summary: Proposes a Telnet Data Entry Terminal (DET) option for the DODIIS implementation, intended to be compatible with the DET option in RFC 732. It updates RFC 732, was a proposed standard, and invited discussion.

eli5.summary: Some computer terminals work like forms with boxes to fill in. This option teaches Telnet how to carry those forms across a connection.

questions: what is the telnet data entry terminal option
how does telnet support data entry terminals
how do telnet forms terminals work
subtitle: How Telnet carries full-screen forms between terminals and host applications on DODIIS networks.

tldr.problem: Independently built implementations of the Telnet Data Entry Terminal (DET) option from RFC 732 might not interoperate, and character-at-a-time Telnet is costly on the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the DODIIS DET model: a forms terminal with an 80 by 24 default screen, fields with attributes, function keys and a set of numbered subcommands, negotiated as Telnet option 20.
tldr.outcome: It records the agreements of DODIIS implementors and updates RFC 732. It was published as a proposed protocol, with discussion and suggestions for improvement encouraged.

today: RFC 1043 is a Proposed Standard from February 1988 that updates RFC 732. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
In the early 1980s the Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) set out to give users Telnet access to full-screen applications across a packet switching network. It did so by implementing Data Entry Terminal (DET) options within Telnet, based on RFC 732. The Department of Defense Intelligence Information System (DODIIS) is a confederation of heterogeneous computer systems and remote terminals that uses the Defense Data Network as its backbone.

Full-screen Telnet is more efficient than character-echo Telnet, where each key press produces a datagram of TCP/IP headers plus one character and the host echoes a similar datagram back. In the DODIIS community, full-screen applications are highly encouraged, line at a time is acceptable and character remote echo is discouraged.

The DET option was chosen in 1981 for DODIIS forms applications and terminals. Because several organizations built it independently, implementors met and wrote down their agreements and recommendations in this document.
sections.eli5: Typing one letter at a time and waiting for each to bounce back is slow. Sending a whole form at once is faster, so everyone agreed on one way to do it.

sections.title: Negotiating the DET Option
sections.content:
The option name is DET and its option code is 20. It is requested with DO DET and WILL DET and accepted by the matching replies, and it must be negotiated in both directions. A WONT DET or DONT DET demands a return to Telnet NVT mode if DET is active, or refuses to start DET mode. If DET cannot be negotiated, the connection is not run in DET mode.

Several other options conflict with DET, so when it is negotiated Echo, Suppress Go-Ahead and Binary should be refused or explicitly terminated.

After that, facility subcommands negotiate which subcommands and attributes may be used. The terminal states what it provides and the application states what it wants. The usable set is the logical intersection of the facility maps sent and received, and for intensity the lesser number of levels wins. Either side may start the negotiation: the initiator needs no reply to the answer, while the other side must respond. Either party may disable a facility at any time by sending the facility subcommand again. Reserved bits must be zeroed to show non-support.

A minimal implementation consists of the subcommands usable without negotiation: the four facilities subcommands, MOVE-CURSOR, HOME-CURSOR, ERASE-SCREEN, TRANSMIT-SCREEN, FORMAT-DATA, ERROR and the two out-of-context subcommands.
sections.eli5: Before playing a game, both players check which rules they both know. Only the rules both sides know are used, and either side can say 'let us stop using that one'.

sections.title: The DODIIS Terminal Model
sections.content:
The model is a half-duplex, forms-oriented device. It has a rectangular screen that shows protected and unprotected data (a form), with optional blinking, reverse video and up to seven display intensity levels. It has a keyboard for editing unprotected fields, function keys that the application can enable or disable one at a time, and a field selection device similar to a light pen.

The default screen is 80 characters by 24 lines, changeable through the Output Line Width and Output Page Size options. Terminal hosts agree to support page sizes of 24 to 48 lines and 64 function keys, numbered 0 through 63. The cursor position is (x,y), where x runs from 0 to M-1 and y from 0 to N-1. Field data is limited to displayable ASCII codes 32 through 126 plus code 7 (BELL).

The model does not support character editors or basic scrolling applications.
sections.eli5: Think of a paper form on a clipboard. Some boxes are printed and cannot be changed, and others are blank for you to write in.

sections.title: DET Subcommands
sections.content:
Each subcommand is sent as IAC SB DET <code> ... IAC SE. They fall into groups: facilities, edit, transmit, erase, format and miscellaneous.

FORMAT-DATA (code 36) defines a field at the cursor with a two-byte format map and a two-byte count giving the field size. The map holds blinking, reverse video, right justification, a two-bit protection value (0 none, 1 protected, 2 alphabetic-only, 3 numeric-only), three bits of intensity, and the Modified and Selectable flags. A field is at least one character. REPEAT (37) compresses runs of identical characters.

The application asks for data with TRANSMIT-SCREEN (20), TRANSMIT-UNPROTECTED (21) or TRANSMIT-MODIFIED (27), and the terminal marks the returned fields with DATA-TRANSMIT (28) and FIELD-SEPARATOR (39). FUNCTION-KEY (40) reports a key press, ENABLE-FUNCTION-KEYS (44) uses two bits per key to disable it or enable it with or without returning screen data, and SELECTED-FIELD (45) reports a field selection. The RFC also warns that parameter bytes may equal the IAC value and must then be doubled.
sections.eli5: Each subcommand is a short instruction card, like 'move the pen here' or 'make this box a numbers-only box'. Each card has a number so both sides know which one it is.

sections.title: Building Forms and Reading Responses
sections.content:
The application builds a form on an erased screen by defining fields by start position, size, attributes and contents. It may build in any order, fields may not overlap, and overwriting a field to change it is allowed. It then sends a transmit subcommand to say what it wants back, preferring TRANSMIT-MODIFIED to keep data volume low, and sends GO-AHEAD to unlock the keyboard.

The user edits the unprotected fields and signals form-complete, presses an enabled function key or selects a field. The terminal then sends the response and returns GO-AHEAD. If no transmit subcommand was sent, the terminal assumes TRANSMIT-MODIFIED when the Modified attribute was negotiated, TRANSMIT-UNPROTECTED when only Protection was, and TRANSMIT-SCREEN otherwise. With TRANSMIT-MODIFIED, fields carrying the Modified attribute are returned as well as those the user changed.

A repeated FIELD-SEPARATOR means a field was unchanged and not returned. Field selection does not itself send GO-AHEAD.
sections.eli5: The host hands you a form and says 'your turn'. You fill in the boxes, press a button, and only the boxes you changed go back.

sections.title: Line Discipline and Out-of-Context Data
sections.content:
In DET mode, GO-AHEAD is never passed implicitly. When DET is negotiated the application holds it. While the application holds GO-AHEAD, the terminal may send only the Telnet commands INTERRUPT-PROCESS, ABORT-OUTPUT, BREAK and ARE-YOU-THERE. While the terminal holds it, the application may send only out-of-context data, or MOVE-CURSOR and FORMAT-DATA to update protected fields. These rules are stricter than the NVT rules in MIL-STD-1782 and apply only in DET mode.

Out-of-context data, bracketed by START-OUT-OF-CONTEXT-DATA (42) and END-OUT-OF-CONTEXT-DATA (43), is shown without disturbing the form, for example replies to ARE-YOU-THERE or host messages. It is display only and has no user reply. If the application needs the GO-AHEAD back, it should send such a message asking the user to enter form-complete. The Telnet ERASE CHARACTER and ERASE LINE functions are not required and should not be sent in DET mode.
sections.eli5: It is like a talking stick: only the one holding it may speak. The host can still slip a short note onto the screen without taking the stick.

sections.title: Error Reporting
sections.content: The ERROR subcommand (41) carries the code of the offending subcommand and one of 13 error codes, for example 1 for a facility not previously negotiated, 3 for a cursor address out of bounds and 13 for an invalid field because of overlap. Errors should be reported when detected, but the implementation should still try to carry out the intent of the offending subcommand or data. An unsupported combination of format attributes should not cause the session to end. The closing implementation note is the robustness principle: be conservative in what you send and liberal in what you accept.
sections.eli5: If someone gives a confusing instruction, you tell them what was wrong but still try your best to do what they meant.
